title: Longest Common Subsequence
problem: Given two strings text1 and text2, return the length of their longest common subsequence. A subsequence keeps the relative order of characters but can skip any of them. If there is none, return 0.
example: Explanation: "ace" is a subsequence of both strings.
intuition: Look at the first character of each string. If text1[i] == text2[j], the best thing to do is use that pair: the answer is 1 + LCS(rest, rest). If they differ, at least one of the two characters is not in the answer, so try dropping each one and take the better: max(LCS(i+1, j), LCS(i, j+1)).

That gives f(i, j) = LCS of text1[i..] and text2[j..]. There are only n * m distinct (i, j) pairs, but plain recursion visits them again and again, which is why we cache. This exact "match → move both, mismatch → try skipping each" shape is the parent of Edit Distance, Distinct Subsequences, Wildcard, and many more today.
notes: Say it like this: "Plain recursion tries skipping a character from either string on every mismatch, so it is exponential. There are only n times m distinct (i, j) states, so memoizing or filling a bottom-up table gives O(n·m) time. Since each row depends only on the previous row, I can cut space to O(m)."
Edge cases: one empty string (answer 0); identical strings (answer n); no common characters.
Common mistakes: off-by-one between dp indices and string indices (dp[i][j] uses charAt(i-1)); forgetting to swap rows; on a match, also taking max with the skip options is harmless but unnecessary.

Follow-ups: "Print the LCS" — fill the full table, then walk back from dp[n][m]: on a match take the char and go diagonal, else move toward the larger neighbour. "Shortest common supersequence" — its length is n + m - LCS. 13.2
simple: Find the length of the longest sequence of letters that appears in both strings in the same order (gaps allowed).

approaches.label: Brute Force (Recursion)
steps: f(i, j) returns 0 if either string is used up.
If characters match, return 1 + f(i+1, j+1).
Otherwise return max(f(i+1, j), f(i, j+1)).
approaches.why: Each mismatch branches into two calls, and the recursion depth is at most n + m.
approaches.simple: Compare the current letters. If they match, count 1 and move both forward; if not, try skipping a letter from one string or the other.

approaches.label: Better (Memoization)
steps: Same recursion, plus a memo[n][m] table filled with -1.
Before computing f(i, j), return the cached value if it exists.
approaches.why: Each of the n * m states is computed once with O(1) work; the memo table plus recursion stack is O(n * m + n + m).
approaches.simple: Same recursion, but store each (i, j) answer so it is worked out only once.

approaches.label: Optimal (Tabulation → Space-Optimized)
steps: dp[i][j] = LCS of the first i chars of text1 and the first j chars of text2. Row 0 and column 0 are 0 (empty string).
If text1[i-1] == text2[j-1], dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1], else max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
Row i only reads row i-1, so keep just two 1D arrays prev and cur.
approaches.space: O(n * m) for the table, O(m) after the space optimisation
approaches.why: We fill each cell once; the optimised version only stores the previous and current rows. Tabulation:
approaches.simple: Fill a table where each cell is the answer for two prefixes; then shrink it to two rows because each row needs only the one above.

title: Longest Common Substring
problem: Given two strings s1 and s2, return the length of the longest string that appears as a contiguous substring in both. (GFG: "Longest Common Substring".)
example: Explanation: "CDGH" is the longest common substring.
intuition: The difference from LCS is "contiguous". A substring cannot skip characters, so on a mismatch the run simply breaks: the length of the common run ending there becomes 0. Define dp[i][j] = length of the longest common substring that ends exactly at s1[i-1] and s2[j-1]. If the characters match, the run extends the diagonal: dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]; otherwise dp[i][j] = 0. The answer is the maximum cell anywhere in the table, not dp[n][m].
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force tries every pair of starting points and extends, O(n·m·min). The DP stores the length of the common run ending at each (i, j): extend the diagonal on a match, reset to 0 on a mismatch, and take the maximum over all cells. That is O(n·m) time and O(m) space with two rows."
Edge cases: empty string; no common characters (0); one string inside the other (answer = shorter length).
Common mistakes: returning dp[n][m] instead of the global max; copying LCS and writing max(up, left) on a mismatch (that turns it back into subsequence).

Follow-ups: "Return the substring" — remember the i where best was updated; the answer is s1.substring(i - best, i). For very long strings, a suffix automaton or binary search + rolling hash gives near-linear time. 13.3
simple: Find the longest piece of text that appears unbroken in both strings.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For every pair of start positions (i, j), extend k while s1[i+k] == s2[j+k].
Track the largest k.
approaches.why: There are n * m start pairs and each extension can run up to min(n, m) characters.
approaches.simple: For every pair of starting points, count how far the two strings keep matching.

approaches.label: Optimal (Tabulation → Space-Optimized)
steps: dp[i][j] = length of the common run ending at s1[i-1], s2[j-1].
Match → 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]; mismatch → 0. Update best at every cell.
Only the previous row is read, so use two 1D arrays (shown below; the full table is the same loop with dp[i] [j]).
approaches.why: Each cell is O(1) work, and we only keep the previous and current rows.
approaches.simple: dp cell = length of the matching run ending at these two letters; a mismatch resets it to 0. Track the biggest cell.

title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence
problem: Given a string s, return the length of its longest subsequence that reads the same forwards and backwards.
example: Explanation: "bbbb" is a palindromic subsequence of length 4.
intuition: Look at both ends of the range s[i..j]. If s[i] == s[j], they can be the outer pair of the palindrome: 2 + f(i+1, j-1). If they differ, at least one end is not used: max(f(i+1, j), f(i, j-1)). Base cases: i > j gives 0 and i == j gives 1.

A neat alternative: the longest palindromic subsequence of s equals LCS(s, reverse(s)). Mention it — it shows you see the connection — but the interval form is just as short and avoids building the reversed string.
notes: Say it like this: "Recursion on the two ends: if they match, take both; if not, drop one end. That is exponential alone, O(n²) with memoization over (i, j) intervals, and I can tabulate it from the bottom row up with two 1D arrays for O(n) space. Equivalently, it is the LCS of the string and its reverse."
Edge cases: single character (1); all same characters (n); prev[j-1] when j-1 == i reads row i+1 at column i, which is 0 (empty interval) — correct.
Common mistakes: filling i upward (then dp[i+1] is not ready); confusing with Longest Palindromic Substring (contiguous).
Follow-ups: "Minimum insertions (or deletions) to make the string a palindrome" — n - LPS(s). 13.4
simple: Longest sequence that reads the same both ways, picked from the string with gaps allowed.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Recursion)
steps: f(i, j): return 0 if i > j, 1 if i == j.
Ends match → 2 + f(i+1, j-1); else max(f(i+1, j), f(i, j-1)).
approaches.why: Every mismatch branches into two calls; depth is at most n.
approaches.simple: If the two ends match, they wrap around a palindrome of the inside; otherwise drop one end and try both.

approaches.label: Better (Memoization)
steps: Cache f(i, j) in an n x n table.
approaches.why: There are about n²/2 valid intervals, each solved once in O(1).
approaches.simple: Same recursion with a memo table.

approaches.label: Optimal (Tabulation, Space-Optimized)
steps: dp[i][j] depends on rows i+1 and the same row, so fill i from n-1 down to 0 and j from i+1 up.
Keep only prev (row i+1) and cur (row i). Set cur[i] = 1.
Match → cur[j] = 2 + prev[j-1]; else cur[j] = max(prev[j], cur[j-1]).
approaches.why: We still visit every interval once, but store just two rows of length n.
approaches.simple: Fill the table bottom-up, keeping only the current and next row.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
problem: Given a string s, return the longest contiguous substring that is a palindrome. If several have the same length, any one is accepted.
example: Explanation: "aba" is also a valid answer.
intuition: Every palindrome has a center. For odd length the center is one character; for even length it is the gap between two characters. So there are only 2n - 1 centers. From each center, expand outward while the two ends match. That checks all palindromes in O(n²) total without any extra memory.
The DP view is also worth knowing: s[i..j] is a palindrome if s[i] == s[j] and s[i+1..j-1] is a palindrome. It gives the same O(n²) time but needs an n x n table.
notes: Say it like this: "Checking every substring is O(n³). A DP table on 'is s[i..j] a palindrome' gets O(n²) time but O(n²) space. Expanding around each of the 2n−1 centers is also O(n²) time but only O(1) space, so that is what I would code."
Edge cases: length 1; all same characters; even-length answers like "cbbd" → "bb" (forgetting even centers breaks this).
Common mistakes: computing start wrongly — for a palindrome of length cur centered at i (or i, i+1), start = i - (cur - 1) / 2 works for both.
Follow-ups: "Can you do O(n)?" — Manacher's algorithm reuses mirror information to get linear time; you rarely need to code it, but name it. 13.5
simple: Find the longest continuous piece of the string that is a palindrome.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For every substring s[i..j], check whether it is a palindrome with two pointers.
Keep the longest one.
approaches.why: There are O(n²) substrings and each check is O(n).
approaches.simple: Check every substring with two pointers.

approaches.label: Better (DP Table)
steps: dp[i][j] = true if s[i..j] is a palindrome.
Fill i from right to left so dp[i+1][j-1] is ready: dp[i][j] = s[i]==s[j] && (j - i < 3 || dp[i+1][j- 1]).
Track the longest true cell.
approaches.why: Each cell is O(1), but we store the whole table.
approaches.simple: A piece is a palindrome if its ends match and its inside is a palindrome; fill a table of yes/no answers.

approaches.label: Optimal (Expand Around Center)
steps: For each index i, expand from (i, i) for odd length and (i, i+1) for even length.
Expansion stops when ends differ or go out of bounds; the palindrome length is r - l - 1.
Keep the best start and length.
approaches.why: 2n - 1 centers, each expanding up to O(n); only a few integer variables are stored.
approaches.simple: Every palindrome has a centre. Grow outward from each centre (one letter or between two letters) while the ends match.

title: Palindromic Substrings
problem: Given a string s, return how many of its substrings are palindromes. Substrings at different positions count separately even if they contain the same characters.
intuition: Same idea as the previous problem, but instead of keeping the longest we count. Every successful step of an expansion from a center is one more palindrome: if s[l] == s[r], then s[l..r] is a palindrome, count it, then try one wider.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force checks all O(n²) substrings in O(n) each. A palindrome DP table brings it to O(n²) time and space. Expanding around the 2n−1 centers and counting each successful step is O(n²) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: single char (1); string with all distinct chars (answer n).
Common mistakes: forgetting even-length centers; counting distinct palindromes instead of positions.
Follow-ups: "Count distinct palindromic substrings" — needs a set of strings (or a palindromic tree / eertree). Manacher's also counts in O(n): sum of (radius + 1) / 2 style terms. 13.6
simple: Count how many substrings are palindromes.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For every substring, check palindrome with two pointers and count.
approaches.why: O(n²) substrings, O(n) per check.
approaches.simple: Check every substring.

approaches.label: Better (DP Table)
steps: dp[i][j] = s[i]==s[j] && (j - i < 3 || dp[i+1][j-1]), filling i from right to left.
Count true cells.
approaches.why: One O(1) check per cell, full table stored.
approaches.simple: Fill the yes/no palindrome table and count the yeses.

approaches.label: Optimal (Expand Around Center)
steps: For each center (odd (i, i) and even (i, i+1)), expand while the ends match.
Add 1 for every successful expansion step.
approaches.why: 2n − 1 centers, each expanding O(n) at most, constant extra memory.
approaches.simple: Expand around every centre and count each successful step outward.

title: Edit Distance
problem: Given two strings word1 and word2, return the minimum number of operations to turn word1 into word2. Allowed operations on word1: insert a character, delete a character, or replace a character.
example: Explanation: horse -> rorse (replace h with r) -> rose (delete r) -> ros (delete e)
intuition: Let f(i, j) = cost to turn word1[i..] into word2[j..]. If the current characters match, do nothing: f(i+1, j+1). Otherwise try all three operations, each costing 1: - Insert word2[j] before word1[i]: now word2[j] is satisfied → f(i, j+1). - Delete word1[i] → f(i+1, j). - Replace word1[i] with word2[j] → f(i+1, j+1).
Base cases tell the story: if word1 is used up, we must insert the remaining m - j characters; if word2 is used up, we must delete the remaining n - i.
notes: Say it like this: "At each pair of positions, if the characters match I move both; otherwise I try insert, delete and replace, each costing one. Plain recursion is O(3^(n+m)); memoizing the n·m states makes it O(n·m), and the bottom-up table only needs the previous row, so space drops to O(m)."
Edge cases: either string empty (answer is the other's length); identical strings (0).

Common mistakes: wrong base row/column (must be i and j, not 0); in the 1D version forgetting cur[0] = i; mixing up which neighbour is insert vs delete (it does not change the answer, but explain it right).
Follow-ups: "Only insert and delete allowed" — answer is n + m - 2·LCS. "Reconstruct the operations" — keep the full table and walk back from dp[n][m]. 13.7
simple: Fewest insert, delete or replace operations to turn one word into another.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Recursion)
steps: Base: i == n → m - j; j == m → n - i.
Match → f(i+1, j+1).
Else 1 + min(insert, delete, replace).
approaches.why: Each mismatch branches three ways; recursion depth is at most n + m.
approaches.simple: If letters match, move on for free; otherwise try insert, delete and replace, each costing 1.

approaches.label: Better (Memoization)
steps: Cache f(i, j) in an n x m table.
approaches.why: n·m states, O(1) each; memo table plus stack.
approaches.simple: Same recursion with a memo.

approaches.label: Optimal (Tabulation → Space-Optimized)
steps: dp[i][j] = edit distance between the first i chars of word1 and the first j of word2. dp[i][0] = i, dp[0][j] = j.
Match → dp[i-1][j-1]; else 1 + min(dp[i][j-1] (insert), dp[i-1][j] (delete), dp[i-1][j-1] (replace)).
Keep only prev and cur rows; remember cur[0] = i.
approaches.why: One pass over the table; the optimised form keeps two rows. Tabulation:
approaches.simple: Fill the table of prefix answers row by row, then keep only two rows.

title: Distinct Subsequences
problem: Given strings s and t, return the number of distinct subsequences of s that equal t (i.e. the number of ways to pick positions in s that spell t). The answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer.
example: Explanation: there are three ways to choose which of the three 'b's to drop.
intuition: Let f(i, j) = number of ways to form t[j..] from s[i..]. If t is finished (j == m), there is exactly 1 way (pick nothing more). If s is finished first, 0 ways. At each step we can always skip s[i]: f(i+1, j). If s[i] == t[j], we can also use it: f(i+1, j+1). Because we are counting, we add the two choices instead of taking a max.
notes: Say it like this: "For each position I can always skip the character in s, and if it matches t I can also use it, and I add those counts. Recursion is exponential; memoizing (i, j) gives O(n·m). Bottom-up, each row only needs the previous one, and iterating j backwards lets me use a single array of size m+1."
Edge cases: t empty → 1; t longer than s → 0.
Common mistakes: looping j left-to-right in the 1D version (uses the current row's value, overcounting); returning 0 instead of 1 when t is exhausted.

Follow-ups: "Overflow?" — intermediate counts can exceed 32 bits even when the final answer fits. In Java, int addition wraps modulo 2³², and since we only add, the final value is still correct; using long (or a modulus, as on GFG with 1e9+7) makes the intent explicit. 13.8
simple: How many different ways can t be picked out of s as a subsequence?

approaches.label: Brute Force (Recursion)
steps: ways = f(i+1, j); if match, ways += f(i+1, j+1).
approaches.why: Each match branches twice; depth is at most n.
approaches.simple: At each letter of s, either skip it or (if it matches) use it for the next letter of t.

approaches.label: Better (Memoization)
steps: Cache f(i, j).
approaches.why: n·m states each computed once.
approaches.simple: Same with a memo.

approaches.label: Optimal (Tabulation → 1D Array)
steps: dp[i][j] = ways to form the first j chars of t from the first i chars of s. dp[i][0] = 1 for all i.
Row i reads row i-1 at j and j-1. With a single array, loop j from right to left so dp[j-1] still holds the previous row's value.
approaches.why: Each cell is O(1); one array of length m + 1.
approaches.simple: One array over t, updated from right to left for each letter of s.

title: Interleaving String
problem: Given strings s1, s2, s3, return whether s3 can be formed by interleaving s1 and s2: all characters of both are used, and each keeps its own internal order.
example: Explanation: take "aa" from s1, "dbbc" from s2, "bc" from s1, "a" from s2, "c" from s1.
intuition: If we have used i chars of s1 and j of s2, the next char of s3 is at k = i + j — so (i, j) fully describes the state. The next character of s3 must come either from s1[i] or from s2[j]. f(i, j) is true if either matching choice leads to success. First check n + m == s3.length(); otherwise the answer is immediately false.
Greedy does not work: when both s1[i] and s2[j] match s3[k], picking the wrong one can fail later, which is exactly why we need DP.
notes: Say it like this: "The state is how many characters I've taken from each string; the position in s3 is their sum. Recursion tries taking the next char from s1 or s2 and is exponential; memoizing the (i, j) grid makes it O(n·m). Bottom-up needs only one row, so O(m) space."
Edge cases: length mismatch → false immediately; all three empty → true; one of s1 / s2 empty → compare directly.
Common mistakes: using a third index k as part of the state (redundant); greedy choice; forgetting the length check, which leads to index out of bounds on s3.
Follow-ups: "O(min(n, m)) space" — swap so the shorter string is on the column axis. 13.9
simple: Can s3 be made by weaving s1 and s2 together, keeping each one's order?

approaches.label: Brute Force (Recursion)
steps: If lengths do not add up, return false.
f(i, j): if i == n && j == m, true.
approaches.why: Each step can branch two ways; depth is n + m.
approaches.simple: At each step take the next letter of s3 from s1 or from s2 if it matches, and recurse.

approaches.label: Better (Memoization)
steps: Cache f(i, j) in a Boolean[n+1][m+1] (null = not computed).
approaches.why: (n+1)(m+1) states, O(1) each.
approaches.simple: Same with a memo.

approaches.label: Optimal (Tabulation, 1D)
steps: dp[i][j] = can the first i of s1 and first j of s2 form the first i+j of s3. dp[0][0] = true.
With one array: dp[j] before update is "from above" (row i-1), and dp[j-1] is already the current row ("from left").
approaches.why: Every cell once; a single row of booleans.
approaches.simple: A 1D table of "can these prefixes form this prefix of s3?" filled row by row.

title: Wildcard Matching
problem: Given a string s and a pattern p, return whether p matches the entire s. In p, '?' matches any single character and '*' matches any sequence of characters, including the empty one.
example: Explanation: first '*' matches "", 'a' matches 'a', second '*' matches "dce", 'b' matches 'b'.
intuition: f(i, j) = does p[j..] match s[i..]. If p[j] is a letter or '?', it must consume exactly one character of s. A '*' has two choices: - match empty: skip the star → f(i, j+1); - match one more char: consume s[i] but keep the star → f(i+1, j).

Those two choices together cover "any number of characters". Base cases: if the pattern is done, s must also be done. If s is done but the pattern is not, the rest of the pattern must be all '*' — which the recursion handles via the "match empty" branch.
notes: Say it like this: "A star either matches nothing, so I skip it, or matches one more character, so I consume from s and keep the star. Recursion is exponential; memoizing (i, j) makes it O(n·m), and the bottom-up version only needs two rows, O(m) space."
Edge cases: pattern of only * matches everything; empty s with pattern "**" → true; empty pattern with non-empty s → false.
Common mistakes: looping over every possible length for * (O(n) per state, O(n²m) total) instead of the two- choice trick; forgetting that leftover * s can match empty at the end.

Follow-ups: "O(1) space?" — the greedy two-pointer method: remember the last * position and the s index it matched to; on mismatch, backtrack to that star and let it eat one more char. Usually fast, O(n·m) worst case. 13.10
simple: Match text against a pattern where ? is any one letter and * is any run of letters.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Recursion)
steps: j == m → return i == n.
approaches.why: Every star branches twice; depth is at most n + m.
approaches.simple: Recurse: * either matches nothing or eats one more letter; other characters must match one letter.

approaches.label: Better (Memoization)
steps: Cache f(i, j) in a Boolean[n+1][m+1].
approaches.why: (n+1)(m+1) states, O(1) work each.
approaches.simple: Same with a memo.

approaches.label: Optimal (Tabulation, Space-Optimized)
steps: Same recurrence bottom-up from the end: dp[i][j] for i from n down to 0 and j from m-1 down to 0. dp[n][m] = true, dp[i][m] = false for i < n.
Row i reads row i+1 (next) and itself, so keep two arrays.
approaches.why: Every cell computed once; only rows i and i+1 stored.
approaches.simple: Fill the table from the ends backwards, keeping two rows.

title: Regular Expression Matching
problem: Given a string s and a pattern p, implement matching with '.' (any single character) and '*' (zero or more of the preceding element). The match must cover the entire string.
example: Explanation: "c*" matches zero c's, "a*" matches "aa", "b" matches "b".
intuition: The key difference from Wildcard: * is glued to the character before it, so look at p[j] and p[j+1] together. Let first = "does s[i] match p[j] " (i < n and p[j] is. or equals s[i]). - If p[j+1] == '*': either use the pair zero times → f(i, j+2), or, if first, use it once more and keep the pair → f(i+1, j). - Otherwise: first && f(i+1, j+1).

Base case: pattern finished → s must be finished. When s is finished but the pattern is not, patterns like "a*b*" can still match via the zero-times branch, so we cannot stop early just because i == n.
notes: Say it like this: "I treat 'x' as one unit: either skip it entirely or, if x matches the current character, consume that character and stay on 'x'. Plain recursion is exponential, memoizing on (i, j) is O(n·m) time and space, and the bottom-up table is the same complexity without recursion."
Edge cases: s = "", p = "a*" → true; p = ".*" matches anything; s = "aa", p = "a" → false (must match the whole string).

Common mistakes: treating * like Wildcard's *; checking first before handling the zero-times branch (zero- times must be allowed even when first is false); reading p[j+1] out of bounds; dp[i+1][j] when i == n — guarded because first is false then.
Follow-ups: "How is this different from Wildcard?" — in Wildcard * stands alone and matches any sequence; here it repeats the previous token. Also "support + " — x+ = x x*. Best Time to Buy And 13.11
simple: Match text against a pattern where . is any letter and x* means zero or more x.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Recursion)
steps: j == m → i == n.
Compute first.
If next is *: f(i, j+2) || (first && f(i+1, j)); else first && f(i+1, j+1).
approaches.why: Each x* branches twice; depth at most n + m.
approaches.simple: If the next pattern char is *, either skip the pair or (if the first letter matches) use it and stay; otherwise match one letter.

approaches.label: Better (Memoization)
steps: Cache f(i, j) in Boolean[n+1][m+1].
approaches.why: (n+1)(m+1) states, constant work each.
approaches.simple: Same with a memo.

approaches.label: Optimal (Tabulation)
steps: dp[i][j] = does p[j..] match s[i..]. dp[n][m] = true.
Fill i from n down to 0 and j from m-1 down to 0 with the same recurrence.
approaches.why: Each cell once. (It can be cut to two rows like Wildcard, but interviewers usually stop here.)
approaches.simple: Fill the yes/no table from the end of both strings backwards.

title: Best Time to Buy And Sell Stock With Cooldown
problem: prices[i] is the stock price on day i. You may complete as many transactions as you like, but you can hold at most one share at a time, and after you sell you must wait one day (cooldown) before buying again. Return the maximum profit.
example: Explanation: buy, sell, cooldown, buy, sell -> (2-1) + (2-0) = 3.
intuition: On any day, the only thing that matters for future decisions is "am I allowed to buy (not holding) or am I holding a share?". So the state is (day, canBuy). - If I can buy: either buy (-prices[i], then I'm holding) or skip. - If I'm holding: either sell (+prices[i], and the cooldown means the next decision day is i + 2) or skip.
The cooldown is just "jump to i + 2 after selling". Everything else is the classic unlimited-transactions stock DP.
notes: Say it like this: "The state is the day plus whether I'm holding. Recursion over buy/skip and sell/skip is exponential; with memoization it is O(n) states. Because each day only looks one or two days ahead, I can run a three-state machine — hold, sold, rest — in O(n) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: one day (0); strictly decreasing prices (0).
Common mistakes: buying from sold instead of rest (breaks the cooldown); updating hold, sold, rest in place without saving old values.
Follow-ups: "Cooldown of k days" — sell jumps to i + k + 1, or keep a small queue of past sold values. Best Time to Buy and Sell 13.12
simple: Buy and sell many times, but after selling you must rest one day. Maximise profit.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Recursion)
steps: f(i, canBuy): if i >= n, return 0.
canBuy → max(-p[i] + f(i+1, false), f(i+1, true)).
holding → max(p[i] + f(i+2, true), f(i+1, false)).
approaches.why: Two choices per day; recursion depth n.
approaches.simple: Each day choose: buy/skip when free, sell/hold when holding. Selling jumps two days ahead.

approaches.label: Better (Memoization)
steps: Cache f(i, canBuy) in an n x 2 table.
approaches.why: 2n states, O(1) each.
approaches.simple: Same choices cached by (day, holding).

approaches.label: Optimal (Space-Optimized State Machine)
approaches.lead: Bottom-up, day i needs only days i+1 and i+2, so a constant number of variables is enough. The forward version reads most naturally as three states at the end of each day:
steps: hold = best profit while holding a share; sold = best profit if I sold today; rest = best profit while not holding and free to buy.
For each price: hold = max(hold, rest - p) (buy only from rest, which enforces the cooldown), sold = hold_old + p, rest = max(rest, sold_old).
Answer is max(sold, rest).
approaches.why: One pass with three variables.
approaches.simple: Track three running states: holding, just sold, resting. Update all three each day.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Transaction Fee
problem: prices[i] is the price on day i, and each completed transaction (buy + sell) costs a fixed fee. You can make unlimited transactions but hold at most one share at a time. Return the maximum profit.
example: Explanation: buy at 1, sell at 8 -> 7 - 2 = 5; buy at 4, sell at 9 -> 5 - 2 = 3; total 8.
intuition: Same (day, canBuy) state as unlimited stock trading. The fee is paid once per transaction, so subtract it when selling. That is the only change, and it is what stops us from trading on every small up-tick.
notes: Say it like this: "Same buy/sell state machine as unlimited trading, with the fee subtracted on every sell. Recursion is O(2^n), memoized it's O(n), and since each day depends only on the next, two variables — cash and hold — give O(n) time, O(1) space."
Edge cases: fee larger than any price gain → 0; single day → 0.
Common mistakes: subtracting the fee on both buy and sell (charge it once); returning max(cash, hold) — hold is never better at the end.
Follow-ups: "Greedy?" — yes, there is a greedy that tracks the effective buy price, but the DP is easier to justify. 13.13
simple: Buy and sell as often as you like, paying a fee on each sale. Maximise profit.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Recursion)
steps: f(i, canBuy): i == n → 0.
canBuy → max(-p[i] + f(i+1, 0), f(i+1, 1)).
holding → max(p[i] - fee + f(i+1, 1), f(i+1, 0)).
approaches.why: Two choices per day, depth n.
approaches.simple: Each day choose buy/skip or sell/hold, subtracting the fee when selling.

approaches.label: Better (Memoization)
steps: Cache f(i, canBuy).
approaches.why: 2n states, O(1) each.
approaches.simple: Same choices with a memo.

approaches.label: Optimal (Space-Optimized)
steps: cash = best profit while not holding; hold = best profit while holding.
For each price: cash = max(cash, hold + p - fee), hold = max(hold, cash - p).
Return cash.
approaches.why: One pass, two variables. Using the freshly updated cash inside hold is safe: selling and re-buying on the same day only loses the fee, so it never beats keeping the share.
approaches.simple: Track two numbers: best cash when not holding and when holding.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV
pattern: DP on stocks with transaction limit
problem: Given an integer k and an array prices, return the maximum profit using at most k transactions (each transaction = one buy then one sell). You cannot hold more than one share at a time.
example: Explanation: buy at 2, sell at 6 (+4); buy at 0, sell at 3 (+3).
intuition: Add one more dimension to the stock state: how many transactions are left. State (i, canBuy, cap). A transaction is counted when we sell (decrement cap on sell). When cap == 0, no more profit is possible.

Bottom-up, think of buy[t] = best profit while holding the share of the t-th transaction, and sell[t] = best profit after completing t transactions. The t-th buy is funded by the profit of t-1 completed transactions: buy[t] = max(buy[t], sell[t-1] - p), sell[t] = max(sell[t], buy[t] + p).
notes: Say it like this: "The state is day, holding-or-not, and transactions left; I decrement the count on each sell. Recursion is exponential, memoized it is O(n·k) time and space. Bottom-up I keep buy[t] and sell[t] for t up to k, giving O(n·k) time and O(k) space, and if k ≥ n/2 I fall back to the unlimited-transactions greedy."
Edge cases: k = 0 → 0; empty or one-day prices → 0; huge k (the shortcut avoids a giant array).
Common mistakes: counting a transaction on both buy and sell; initialising buy to 0 (allows "selling" without buying); Integer.MIN_VALUE + p overflow (avoided because buy[t] is updated first).
Follow-ups: Stock III is this with k = 2. It can also be written with a single index 0..2k-1 where even = buy and odd = sell. 13.14
simple: At most k buy-sell transactions. Maximise profit.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Recursion)
steps: f(i, canBuy, cap): if i == n or cap == 0, return 0.
canBuy → max(-p[i] + f(i+1, 0, cap), f(i+1, 1, cap)).
holding → max(p[i] + f(i+1, 1, cap-1), f(i+1, 0, cap)).
approaches.why: Two choices per day, depth n.
approaches.simple: Recursion over (day, holding, transactions left).

approaches.label: Better (Memoization)
steps: Cache in memo[n][2][k+1].
approaches.why: n · 2 · (k+1) states, O(1) each.
approaches.simple: Same with a 3D memo.

approaches.label: Optimal (Tabulation, O(k) Space)
steps: buy[t] starts at negative infinity (not reachable yet), sell[t] at 0.
For each price, for t = 1..k: buy[t] = max(buy[t], sell[t-1] - p), then sell[t] = max(sell[t], buy[t] + p).
Answer sell[k]. Shortcut: if k >= n/2, the limit never binds — just sum every positive daily difference.
approaches.why: For each of n days we update k pairs; the arrays have k + 1 entries.
approaches.simple: Keep best buy[t] and sell[t] for each transaction count and update them every day.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
problem: Given an integer array nums, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.
intuition: Brute force decides take/skip for each element, remembering the last taken value. The O(n²) DP flips the view: dp[i] = length of the LIS ending at i = 1 + max(dp[j]) over j < i with nums[j] < nums[i].

The O(n log n) trick: keep tails[len] = the smallest possible tail value of any increasing subsequence of length len + 1. Smaller tails are always better because they leave more room to extend. For each number, binary- search the first tail >= x and replace it (or append if x is bigger than all). tails stays sorted, and its size is the LIS length. Note: tails itself is not necessarily a real subsequence — only its length is meaningful.
notes: Say it like this: "Take/skip recursion is O(2^n). The classic DP stores the LIS ending at each index and is O(n²). The optimal keeps the smallest tail for each length and binary-searches where each number goes, which is O(n log n) — the length of that tails array is the answer."
Edge cases: one element (1); all equal elements (1, since strictly increasing); already sorted (n).
Common mistakes: using upper bound (<=) instead of lower bound — that would allow equal elements (non- decreasing LIS); claiming tails is the actual subsequence.

Follow-ups: "Print the LIS" — in the O(n²) DP keep parent[i], then walk back from the best index. "Non- decreasing" — use upper bound. Related: Russian Doll Envelopes, Largest Divisible Subset, Longest String Chain, Longest Bitonic Subsequence. 13.15
simple: Find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Recursion)
steps: f(i, prev): best length from index i onward when the last taken index is prev (-1 for none).
Skip nums[i], or take it if prev == -1 || nums[i] > nums[prev].
approaches.why: Each element is taken or skipped; depth n.
approaches.simple: At each number, take it (if bigger than the last taken) or skip it.

approaches.label: Better (O(n²) DP)
steps: dp[i] = 1 initially (the element alone).
For each i, for each j < i with nums[j] < nums[i], dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1).
Answer is max(dp).
approaches.why: Double loop over pairs; one array. (This is the tabulated form of the memoized f(i, prev).)
approaches.simple: dp[i] = longest increasing run ending at i, built from every smaller earlier number.

approaches.label: Optimal (Binary Search on Tails)
steps: Keep a sorted array tails and its size len.
For each x, find the first index with tails[idx] >= x (lower bound).
Set tails[idx] = x; if idx == len, increase len.
approaches.why: One binary search per element over at most n tails.
approaches.simple: Keep the smallest possible tail for each length and use binary search to place each new number.

title: Number of Longest Increasing Subsequences
problem: Given an integer array nums, return the number of longest strictly increasing subsequences (count subsequences by positions).
intuition: Extend the O(n²) LIS DP with a second array. len[i] = length of the LIS ending at i, cnt[i] = how many such subsequences. When looking at j < i with nums[j] < nums[i]: - If len[j] + 1 > len[i], we found a longer way: len[i] = len[j] + 1, cnt[i] = cnt[j] (reset). - If len[j] + 1 == len[i], another way of the same best length: cnt[i] += cnt[j].
Finally, sum cnt[i] over all i whose len[i] equals the global maximum.
notes: Say it like this: "Enumerating every increasing subsequence is exponential. I extend the O(n²) LIS DP with a count array: a longer extension resets the count, an equal-length extension adds to it, and at the end I sum counts for indices that reach the maximum length. O(n²) time, O(n) space."
Edge cases: all equal elements ([2,2,2] → 3, each single element is an LIS of length 1); strictly decreasing → n.
Common mistakes: adding cnt[j] instead of resetting when a longer length is found; returning only cnt[n- 1] instead of summing over all indices with max length.
Follow-ups: "O(n log n)?" — possible with a Fenwick tree / segment tree over compressed values, storing (best length, count) pairs per value; mention it, rarely asked to code. 13.16
simple: How many longest increasing subsequences are there?

approaches.label: Brute Force (Enumerate All Increasing Subsequences)
steps: DFS from every start index, extending to any later larger element.
Every node of the DFS is one increasing subsequence; compare its length to the best and update the best length and count.
approaches.why: In the worst case (sorted input) every subset is increasing and we loop over the remaining elements at each one; depth up to n.
approaches.simple: List every increasing subsequence and count the longest ones.

approaches.label: Optimal (O(n²) DP with Counts)
steps: len[i] = cnt[i] = 1 for all i.
For each i and each j < i with nums[j] < nums[i]: update len / cnt as described.
Sum cnt[i] where len[i] == maxLen.
approaches.why: All pairs (j, i) are examined once; two arrays of size n.
approaches.simple: For each position keep the best length and how many ways reach it; combine from smaller earlier numbers.

title: Matrix Chain Multiplication
problem: You are given an array arr of size n where matrix i (1-based, i = 1..n-1) has dimensions arr[i-1] x arr[i]. Multiplying a p x q matrix by a q x r matrix costs p * q * r scalar multiplications. Return the minimum total cost to multiply the whole chain (you choose the parenthesisation, not the order). (GFG: "Matrix Chain Multiplication".)
intuition: This is the template for partition DP. Let f(i, j) = min cost to multiply matrices i..j. The last multiplication splits the chain at some k (i <= k < j): the left part i..k becomes an arr[i-1] x arr[k] matrix, the right part k+1..j becomes arr[k] x arr[j], and multiplying them costs arr[i-1] * arr[k] * arr[j]. Try every k and take the minimum. A single matrix (i == j) costs 0.

The recipe for every partition DP: (1) define f(i, j) on a range, (2) loop over the split point k, (3) combine the two sub-ranges plus the cost of the split, (4) fill the table by increasing range length (or i from right to left).
notes: Say it like this: "I pick the last multiplication: splitting at k costs the two halves plus arr[i-1]·arr[k]·arr[j]. Trying every split recursively is exponential; memoizing the O(n²) ranges with O(n) splits each gives O(n³) time and O(n²) space, and the bottom-up table fills i from right to left."
Edge cases: arr of length 2 (one matrix) → 0.

Common mistakes: looping k up to j (must stop at j - 1); filling the table row by row from the top (the lower rows are not ready); overflow — with GFG limits (values ≤ 500) int is fine, otherwise use long.

Follow-ups: "Print the parenthesisation" — store the best k in split[i][j] and recurse to print. Same template: Burst Balloons, Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick, Boolean Parenthesization, Palindrome Partitioning. 13.17
simple: Choose the bracket order for multiplying a chain of matrices that costs the fewest multiplications.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Recursion)
steps: f(i, j): if i == j, return 0.
For k in i..j-1: cost = f(i, k) + f(k+1, j) + arr[i-1]*arr[k]*arr[j]; take the min.
Answer f(1, n-1).
approaches.why: The same sub-ranges are solved many times; recursion depth is at most n.
approaches.simple: Try every place to make the last split, recursing on both sides.

approaches.label: Better (Memoization)
steps: Cache f(i, j) in an n x n table.
approaches.why: O(n²) ranges, each trying O(n) split points.
approaches.simple: Same with a memo table.

approaches.label: Optimal (Tabulation)
steps: dp[i][j] = min cost for matrices i..j; dp[i][i] = 0.
dp[i][j] needs dp[i][k] (same row, smaller j) and dp[k+1][j] (lower rows), so loop i from n-1 down to 1 and j from i+1 up to n-1.
approaches.why: Same work as memoization without recursion overhead. No further space reduction is possible here because a cell reads a whole row and a whole column.
approaches.simple: Fill the table for short chains first, then longer ones.

title: Burst Balloons
problem: There are n balloons with numbers nums[i]. Bursting balloon i earns nums[left] * nums[i] * nums[right], where left and right are its current neighbours (treat out-of-range as 1). After bursting, the neighbours become adjacent. Return the maximum coins you can collect by bursting all balloons.
intuition: Choosing which balloon to burst first is a dead end: after it pops, its neighbours change, so the left and right parts are no longer independent. The unlock is to choose which balloon in range [i, j] is burst last. If k is last, then while everything else in [i, j] is popping, k is still standing and acts as a wall, so [i, k-1] and [k+1, j] are independent. When k finally pops, its neighbours are the balloons just outside the range, a[i-1] and a[j+1].

Pad the array with a 1 on each side: a = [1,...nums, 1]. Then f(i, j) = max over k in [i, j] of a[i- 1]*a[k]*a[j+1] + f(i, k-1) + f(k+1, j), with f(i, j) = 0 when i > j. This is Matrix Chain Multiplication in disguise.
notes: Say it like this: "If I pick the first balloon to burst, the subproblems interact. If I pick the last balloon k in a range, it separates the left and right halves, and when it pops its neighbours are the boundaries outside the range. That gives an interval DP: exponential as plain recursion, O(n³) time and O(n²) space with memoization or tabulation."
Edge cases: single balloon → 1 * x * 1; zeros in the array (they still work, just contribute 0).
Common mistakes: thinking "first burst" instead of "last burst"; using a[k-1] / a[k+1] as neighbours instead of the range boundaries a[i-1] / a[j+1]; forgetting the padding.
Follow-ups: "Why does choosing last work?" — because k is the only balloon left at the end, so the left and right parts never see each other's balloons as neighbours. 13.18
simple: Burst balloons to collect left × this × right coins. Get the most coins.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Recursion)
steps: Pad the array.
f(i, j): if i > j return 0; try each k as the last balloon.
Answer f(1, n).
approaches.why: Overlapping ranges are recomputed repeatedly; depth at most n.
approaches.simple: Think backwards: pick which balloon is burst last in a range; its neighbours are the range's borders.

approaches.label: Better (Memoization)
steps: Cache f(i, j) in a (n+2) x (n+2) table.
approaches.why: O(n²) ranges × O(n) choices of k.
approaches.simple: Same with a memo.

approaches.label: Optimal (Tabulation)
steps: dp[i][j] for 1 <= i <= j <= n; cells with i > j stay 0.
Fill i from n down to 1 and j from i up to n, since dp[i][j] needs dp[i][k-1] (same row, smaller j) and dp[k+1][j] (lower row).
approaches.why: Three nested loops over i, j, k; a 2D table.
approaches.simple: Fill the table for small ranges first, growing to the full range.

title: Palindrome Partitioning II
problem: Given a string s, partition it so that every piece is a palindrome. Return the minimum number of cuts needed.
intuition: Think "front partition": standing at index i, choose where the first piece ends (j). If s[i..j] is a palindrome, cut after j and solve the rest: f(i) = min over valid j of 1 + f(j+1), with f(n) = 0. That counts pieces, and the number of cuts is pieces - 1 (the final piece needs no cut after it).
The remaining cost is the palindrome check. Precompute pal[i][j] in O(n²) using the same rule as Longest Palindromic Substring: s[i] == s[j] && (j - i < 2 || pal[i+1][j-1]). Then each check is O(1).
notes: Say it like this: "From each index I choose where the first palindromic piece ends and recurse on the rest; cuts are pieces minus one. Plain recursion is exponential; memoizing on the start index is O(n³) because of the palindrome checks; precomputing a palindrome table makes each check O(1), so the whole thing is O(n²) time and O(n²) space."
Edge cases: whole string is already a palindrome → 0; all distinct characters → n − 1; single character → 0.
Common mistakes: returning pieces instead of cuts; filling pal top-down so pal[i+1][j-1] is not ready; trying every (i, j) split like MCM (O(n³)) instead of front partition.

Follow-ups: "O(n) extra space?" — expand around each center; for every palindrome s[l..r] found, update cut[r+1] = min(cut[r+1], cut[l] + 1). Related: Palindrome Partitioning I (list all partitions, backtracking) and Partition Array for Maximum Sum (same front-partition template).
simple: Fewest cuts so that every piece is a palindrome.

approaches.label: Brute Force (Recursion)
steps: For each j >= i with s[i..j] a palindrome (checked with two pointers), take 1 + f(j+1).
Answer f(0) - 1.
approaches.why: Every cut position can be tried or not; each check is O(n); depth n.
approaches.simple: Try every palindromic first piece and recurse on the rest.

approaches.label: Better (Memoization)
steps: Cache f(i) in an array of size n. Palindrome check is still two pointers.
approaches.why: n states × n choices of j × O(n) palindrome check.
approaches.simple: Same with a memo.

approaches.label: Optimal (Palindrome Table + Tabulation)
steps: Build pal[i][j] with i from n-1 down to 0 and j from i up.
dp[n] = 0; for i from n-1 down to 0: dp[i] = min over j >= i with pal[i][j] of 1 + dp[j+1].
Return dp[0] - 1.
approaches.why: Both the palindrome table and the DP loop are double loops with O(1) work inside; the table is n × n.
approaches.simple: Pre-build a palindrome table, then fill best cuts from the end of the string backwards.
